factor.name: Admin key custody type
factor.scoring_methodology:
**What this measures**
This factor records the categorical type of custody arrangement holding the protocol's most privileged admin role: one of EOA, multisig, multisig-plus-timelock, full DAO-plus-timelock, or immutable (no admin). The value is determined by an on-chain read of the owner, admin, or ProxyAdmin slot on every major deployed contract. The result is a single categorical label that anchors the full governance & admin section — it is the baseline posture description from which more specific factors (RD-F-027 through RD-F-047) derive their context.

**Why it matters**
Admin key custody type is the foundational governance signal — before assessing threshold sizes, timelock durations, or role separation, a depositor needs to know what class of mechanism holds ultimate control. The evidence base shows that every off-chain key compromise incident in the dataset was possible only because the exploited admin role was held by a custody type that could be compromised with a single key or a small coordinated set of keys. Immutable protocols cannot be upgraded by anyone and occupy a different risk category entirely; DAO-plus-timelock protocols have the highest structural resistance to unilateral action; EOA protocols have the lowest. This factor drives the display value on the protocol card and informs which sub-factors are applicable.

**Green / Yellow / Red**
Green is assigned when the highest-privilege admin role is held by a multisig-plus-timelock or full DAO-plus-timelock, with the timelock meeting the minimum duration threshold assessed under RD-F-032. Yellow covers a multisig without timelock or a DAO without timelock. Red is assigned when the admin role is held by a single EOA (which also triggers RD-F-027), or when no admin role can be identified from on-chain data (opacity, not immutability).

**Common gray cases**
This factor is grayed only when proxy architecture obscures the admin slot entirely and no published documentation identifies the governance type — an uncommon state for any protocol with material TVL.

**Notable historical examples**
No cross-hacked incidents currently linked in database for this factor.

scored_protocols.evidence_summary: DAO+timelock custody. Executor Lvl1 (1-day) for routine ops; Executor Lvl2 (7-day) for governance-critical changes; two 5-of-9 Guardian multisigs for emergency actions. No EOA holds any admin role.

scored_protocols.evidence_detail: The official operating manual identifies the Ethereum Across DAO Safe at 0xB524735356985D2f267FA010D681f061DfF03715 as a 3-of-5 Council Safe and states that protocol upgrades remain handled by the Council. The passed AcrossCo/ACX proposal says the protocol continues operating during a transition, while the June 30 update says the exchange portal was delayed for legal and operational work. No public evidence reviewed through 2026-07-30 shows that the pending portal or corporate transition replaced the current on-chain Safe control path.
scored_protocols.evidence_summary: Core administration remains a documented 3-of-5 Across Council Safe without a mandatory timelock for protocol upgrades; the passed AcrossCo/ACX transition and delayed exchange portal have not publicly changed that on-chain control path.

Dual-layer governance: (a) BABY governance via Cosmos SDK x/gov — DAO model with 3-day voting period, 33.4% quorum, >50% threshold; no single admin key; (b) Bitcoin-layer: covenant committee 6-of-9 federated multisig for BTC unbonding co-signing. All software upgrades require on-chain governance vote (MsgSoftwareUpgrade). V2 upgrade (Jun 2025) and V4 upgrade (Nov 2025) both went through governance proposals confirmed by on-chain voting.

Centrifuge documents Root as the immutable administrator of protocol contracts, with privileged escalation subject to a 48-hour delay and governance actions mediated by separate Safe-controlled guardians. The effective custody model is multisig plus timelock.
5-of-8 Gnosis Safe multisig controls upgrades and all admin roles on Ethereum. No timelock. Classification: multisig (without timelock).

The current technical architecture documents four governance multisigs. The Protocol Council executes queued upgrades through the primary timelock, and no single EOA is documented in that upgrade route.

Ethena documents a protocol multisig and a separate Dev Multisig; the public contract and documentation reviewed do not establish an on-chain timelock for the relevant admin path. The documented multisig architecture leaves meaningful key-management risk.

The protocol-admin Safe at 0xcdd57D11476c22d265722F68390b036f3DA48c21 is currently a 6-of-10 Safe. The verified EtherFiTimelock exposes proposer, executor, and delay-controlled execution roles; no single EOA admin path was established from the public sources reviewed.

Bridge2 proxy admin is a Hyper Foundation multisig (undisclosed address, threshold unknown). L1 critical operations require 2/3 stake-weighted cold-validator quorum. Operational parameters controlled by Hyperliquid Labs via closed-source L1 binary. Classification: multisig without timelock on upgrades. Admin type is multisig but transparency is low.

Admin key custody is hybrid: Squads multisig PDA for program upgrades and stake pool manager; JTO DAO (Realms SPL Governance) for protocol-level decisions; Foundation Directors for off-chain/operational decisions. Not a single EOA.

Squads identifies Kamino as a protocol using Squads for program management, which is a multisig workflow. The public material reviewed does not expose the current program authority account, threshold, or a Kamino-specific timelock.
Kelp publishes mixed Safe-plus-timelock custody: its core Ethereum ProxyAdmin is timelock-owned, while a second ProxyAdmin is Admin-Safe-owned.
Full DAO + timelock custody type. Aragon LDO voting → EmergencyProtectedTimelock (3-day min) → AdminExecutor. No single EOA or low-threshold multisig controls protocol upgrades.

Current Lombard documentation states that critical operations require signatures from at least 10 of 14 Consortium members. It does not publish an on-chain mapping from that policy to the reviewed upgrade-admin contracts or identify each role holder, so effective upgrade custody cannot be verified from the available public documentation.
